title: Persona Architecture — Designing How the System Shows Up
content:
An AI persona is not a character sheet. It is a set of behavioural commitments that must hold across thousands of unpredictable interactions.

THE LAYERS, from most to least stable:
1. VALUES — what it will and will not do, and what it prioritises when instructions conflict. Never varies.
2. ROLE — what it is for. Assistant, advisor, collaborator, tool, tutor. Sets the initiative default (see ax-002).
3. VOICE — vocabulary, sentence length, formality, use of humour. Stable across contexts.
4. TONE — the register for a given moment. Varies with the user's state. Warm on success, plain on error, brief when the user is terse.
5. SURFACE STYLE — formatting habits: headers, bullets, emoji, length.

WHAT MAKES A PERSONA WORK:
- SPECIFICITY OVER ADJECTIVES. 'Friendly but professional' is unusable. 'Uses contractions, never exclamation marks, answers before explaining, admits uncertainty in one clause not a paragraph' is implementable and testable.
- WRITTEN AS EXAMPLES. Three good responses and three bad ones for the same input teach more than a page of description, and they double as evaluation cases.
- DEFINED FOR THE HARD MOMENTS, not the easy ones. Any persona works on a successful answer. Define it for: being wrong, being corrected, refusing, not knowing, the user being angry, and the user being upset about something outside the product.
- CONSTRAINED IN LENGTH AND FORMAT. Most perceived personality is actually formatting. A system that returns four bullet points where a sentence would do reads as bureaucratic regardless of its stated voice.

ANTI-PATTERNS:
- Persona as a substitute for capability. Charm does not compensate for wrongness; it makes it worse by increasing trust.
- Persona-driven confidence (see at-001). The character should not determine certainty.
- A persona that cannot be quiet. Anything that adds a greeting, a summary, and an offer of further help to every response is exhausting by the tenth interaction.
- Anthropomorphic overreach — claiming feelings, memory, or relationships it does not have.

title: Tone Calibration — Matching the Moment
content:
Voice is constant; tone varies. Getting tone wrong is the most common way an otherwise good AI product feels tone-deaf.

TONE BY USER STATE:
| State | Tone |
|---|---|
| Exploring | Open, offering options, low commitment |
| Focused, working | Brief, direct, no preamble, no offers of further help |
| Confused | Plain, one step at a time, no jargon, no reassurance theatre |
| Frustrated | Short, acknowledging once, changing approach — not apologising repeatedly |
| Distressed | Human, plain, no cheerfulness, escalate rather than solve |
| Succeeding | Warm and brief. Acknowledge, do not celebrate at length |
| Under time pressure | Answer first, explanation optional and after |

THE RULES:
- MATCH BREVITY. If the user writes three words, do not reply with four paragraphs. Length mirroring is the fastest tone signal there is.
- ANSWER BEFORE EXPLAINING. Preamble is the most common tone failure. 'Great question! There are several factors to consider…' spends the user's attention before delivering anything.
- DROP THE ENTHUSIASM WHEN THINGS FAIL. Cheerfulness during a failure reads as not listening.
- OWN SYSTEM FAILURES IN THE FIRST PERSON; describe user errors without a subject. 'We couldn't reach the server' / 'That email address needs an @'.
- NEVER PERFORM EMOTION. 'I'm so sorry to hear that' from a system the user knows is a system reads as hollow. Plain acknowledgement is more respectful.
- STOP OFFERING HELP. 'Let me know if there's anything else!' on every response is filler that trains users to skip your last line, including when it matters.

CULTURAL CALIBRATION: directness, formality, and the acceptability of humour vary substantially by locale. A tone tuned for US English can read as flippant in Japanese or German business contexts. Where you localise, localise tone deliberately rather than translating the same register.

title: Error Personality — How It Behaves When It Is Wrong
content:
How a system handles being wrong is the highest-leverage trust signal in an AI product. It is also the least designed.

THE FOUR MOMENTS TO DESIGN:
1. IT DOES NOT KNOW. Say so plainly, in one clause, and offer the nearest useful thing. 'I don't know — but I can check X if that helps.' No hedging paragraph.
2. IT WAS WRONG AND THE USER NOTICED. Acknowledge once, correct specifically, do not over-apologise. 'You're right — [correction].' Then move on. Repeated apology signals incompetence.
3. IT WAS WRONG AND THE USER DID NOT NOTICE. If the system detects its own earlier error, it should surface it unprompted. Short-term cost, large long-term trust gain, and almost no product does it.
4. THE USER IS WRONG. Disagree plainly, with the reason, without capitulating. Sycophancy here is worse than disagreement — a system that folds under pushback cannot be relied on for anything.

THE SPECIFIC BEHAVIOURS TO SPECIFY:
- One acknowledgement, not three.
- Correct the specific claim, not the whole answer.
- If it changes position under pushback, NAME the update and the reason. Silent flips are detected and cost more than the original error.
- Do not blame the prompt.
- Do not explain its own limitations at length. One sentence.

WHAT TO WRITE DOWN: for each of the four moments, three approved responses and three rejected ones. This is the most useful page in a persona specification, and it doubles as an evaluation set.

THE STRESS TEST: give it a correct answer, then push back on it three times with increasing insistence but no new evidence. If it caves, your trust design is broken and no amount of confidence language will fix it.

title: Behavioural Consistency — Being the Same System Twice
content:
Consistency is what allows users to build a model of the system. Probabilistic output makes it harder and more important.

WHAT MUST BE CONSISTENT:
- FORMAT PER TASK TYPE. The same kind of request produces the same shape of answer. If a summary is bullets once and prose the next time, the user cannot skim.
- BOUNDARIES. Refusing something it accepted yesterday, or accepting one phrasing of what it refused in another, reads as arbitrary and destroys the user's model.
- PERSONA ACROSS SESSIONS AND SURFACES. The same voice in the chat, the inline suggestion, the error message, and the email.
- TERMINOLOGY. One name per concept, matching the product's UI labels.
- CONFIDENCE LANGUAGE. The same epistemic state expressed the same way.

WHERE VARIATION IS CORRECT: the content of the answer, the specific wording, the level of detail in response to the user's evident need. Users expect creative variation; they do not expect structural variation.

HOW TO GET IT:
- Specify output formats per task type in the system prompt, with examples.
- Use templates for anything structured (see 48).
- Build a regression set: fixed inputs, expected output shapes, run on every prompt change. Prompt edits have non-local effects, and this is the only way to notice.
- Version prompts and record what changed and why (see pa-007).
- Audit across surfaces, not just in the main interface. Error messages and notification copy are where persona drift starts.

THE UNDERRATED FAILURE: consistency between the AI's behaviour and the product's static UI. If the interface calls it a 'workspace' and the assistant calls it a 'project', the user has two models of one thing. Align the model's vocabulary to the UI's labels, not the other way around.

title: Failure Taxonomy — Naming What Goes Wrong
content:
You cannot fix or measure failures you have not named. Build the taxonomy before you build the evaluation.

THE CATEGORIES, for most AI products:
- FACTUALLY WRONG — an assertion that is false.
- CONFIDENTLY WRONG — false and persuasive. Track separately; the harm profile is different.
- INCOMPLETE — right as far as it goes, missing something material.
- IRRELEVANT — answers a question that was not asked.
- MISINTERPRETED — solves the wrong problem correctly.
- FORMAT WRONG — right content, unusable shape.
- REFUSED INCORRECTLY — declined something it should have done. Under-measured and highly damaging.
- OVER-COMPLIED — did something it should have refused or checked first.
- SYCOPHANTIC — agreed with the user against the evidence.
- HEDGED INTO UNUSABILITY — technically correct, practically useless.
- TOO LONG / TOO SHORT — a real failure category, not a nitpick, because it determines whether output gets read.
- STALE — used out-of-date context.
- LOST CONTEXT — ignored something established earlier in the session.
- TOOL FAILURE — the model was fine, the retrieval or the tool was not.
- LATENCY FAILURE — correct but too late to be useful.

HOW TO USE IT:
1. Sample real sessions. Fifty is enough to see the distribution.
2. Classify each failure. Force a single primary category.
3. Count. The distribution is almost always surprising, and almost always different from what the team assumed.
4. Note which categories are model problems, which are prompt problems, which are retrieval problems, and which are INTERFACE problems. In practice a large share are interface problems — format wrong, too long, lost context, incorrectly refused — which is design work.
5. Design the mitigation per category. Not one generic error state.

THIS IS THE ARTEFACT THAT MAKES AI DESIGN WORK MEASURABLE. Without it, quality discussions are anecdote exchange.

title: Output Quality Rubrics — Making 'Good' Checkable
content:
A rubric turns 'that response was better' into something two people can agree on and a system can be graded against.

BUILDING ONE:
1. Pick the task type. Rubrics are per-task; one rubric for 'all outputs' is useless.
2. List the dimensions that matter for THAT task. Typically: correctness, completeness, relevance, format compliance, appropriate length, tone fit, confidence calibration, actionability, and safety.
3. Define each dimension with three anchored levels — fail / acceptable / good — described behaviourally, not with adjectives. 'Good: answers in the first sentence, then supports it' beats 'Good: well-structured'.
4. Weight the dimensions. For a support assistant, correctness and actionability dominate. For a drafting tool, tone and editability do.
5. Write reference examples at each level. The examples are the rubric; the prose is a summary of them.

USING IT:
- Grade a fixed evaluation set before and after every prompt or model change. Without a before, you are guessing.
- Have two people grade the same set independently and compare. Disagreement means the rubric is underspecified, which is useful information.
- Use it as an LLM-judge prompt for scale, but calibrate the judge against human grades first — an uncalibrated judge measures its own preferences.

THE DIMENSIONS MOST OFTEN OMITTED, and most worth including:
- APPROPRIATE LENGTH, because verbosity is the most common real-world quality failure.
- EDITABILITY, because a correct output the user must rewrite has not saved them work.
- CONFIDENCE CALIBRATION, because a confidently wrong answer should score worse than an uncertainly wrong one.
- WHAT IT DID NOT SAY, for anything where omission is the risk.

WHO OWNS THIS: design should, because every one of those dimensions is a design decision expressed as a prompt. If the rubric lives only with engineering, it will measure correctness and nothing else.

title: Measuring an AI Feature — Signals That Mean Something
content:
BEHAVIOURAL SIGNALS, in descending order of honesty:
- ACCEPTANCE RATE — did the user use the output? Copied, kept, committed, sent. The single most informative metric available and usually the easiest to instrument.
- EDIT DISTANCE BEFORE USE — how much did they change it? If users rewrite every output, the feature is generating a first draft, not doing the task, and should be positioned that way.
- RETRY RATE — regeneration or rephrasing. High retry means the first attempt is failing, which no satisfaction survey will tell you.
- ABANDONMENT POINT — where in the interaction people leave.
- TIME TO USEFUL OUTPUT, not time to first token.
- REPEAT USE at 7 and 28 days. Novelty produces excellent week-one numbers for features that die.
- ESCALATION RATE to a human, where applicable.
- CORRECTION PERSISTENCE — do users correct the same thing repeatedly? That is a design failure, not a user failure.

WHAT TO BE SCEPTICAL OF:
- Thumbs up/down. Response rates are low and biased toward extremes, and users learn it does nothing.
- Satisfaction surveys about AI features specifically. Stated attitudes toward AI diverge sharply from behaviour in both directions.
- Engagement time. Longer is not better; for a tool, shorter is usually better.
- Volume of interactions. A user asking five times is a failure, not five successes.

THE HEART MAPPING for AI features: Task success is the primary axis, and it should be defined as 'the user got what they needed', not 'the model returned something'. Adoption and Retention catch the novelty problem. Happiness is the weakest signal here and the one most often reported.

THE QUESTION THAT SETTLES MOST ARGUMENTS: what fraction of outputs are used without modification, and what fraction are abandoned? Instrument that first.
